data.command: Explain T1195.002 supply chain compromise targeting software supply chain

data.text:
webapp@web-srv-01:~$ Explain T1195.002 supply chain compromise targeting software supply chain

T1195.002  Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
Framework     : MITRE ATT&CK (Enterprise)
Tactic        : Initial Access (TA0001)
Parent        : T1195 Supply Chain Compromise
Siblings      : T1195.001 Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
                T1195.003 Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
Platforms     : Linux, macOS, Windows, SaaS, Containers

DESCRIPTION
The adversary modifies a legitimate application before it reaches the victim, inside the
vendor's own build, release or distribution process. Source may be altered before
compilation, or the compiled artifact may be altered after build and before packaging or
delivery. The result is then published through the vendor's normal channel: website,
auto-update endpoint, package repository, marketplace/app store or container registry.
Because the bundle ships from the trusted vendor and is frequently code-signed with the
vendor's own certificate, the victim has little reason to question it. Contrast with
T1195.001, which poisons third-party libraries, dependencies or dev tooling that the
victim assembles itself; T1195.002 is about the finished product or its update path.

Typical insertion points seen in the wild:
    build server or CI runner tampering
    release artifact swap or re-signing
    update mechanism hijack (vendor update server, DNS, CDN or mirror)
    backdoored installer or bootstrapper
    poisoned base image or golden package set

Notable public incidents
    NotPetya (2017)         delivered through backdoored M.E.Doc accounting update
    CCleaner (2017)         trojanized build distributed by the vendor site
    ASUS Live Update (2019) ShadowHammer, signed malicious update
    SolarWinds Orion (2020) SUNBURST inserted in the build pipeline
    Kaseya VSA (2021)       malicious update pushed to managed endpoints
    3CX DesktopApp (2023)   trojanized signed installer/update

WHY IT MATTERS ON A HOST LIKE THIS ONE
A small web application server sits downstream of many suppliers: OS packages, npm and pip
dependencies, container base images, vendor agents and monitoring daemons, plus the CI
pipeline that builds the app itself. Any of those can carry
